codeReview.summary: The feature adds signal handlers, atomic write-rename persistence, and broader cleanup plumbing, but it still misses two core shutdown guarantees: the server does not stop accepting work immediately on signal, and not every Python subprocess created by the server is actually part of shutdown cleanup.

issues.description: `registerShutdownHandlers()` waits on `automationMutex` before `performShutdown()` can call `stopAcceptingConnections()` / `closeWebSocketConnections()` (`server/automation/shutdown.ts:79-82`). The same mutex is held by automation and workflow start/stop routes (`server/automation/routes.ts:43-71`, `server/workflows/routes.ts:113-145`), so after SIGTERM/SIGINT the HTTP listener can continue admitting new requests until an in-flight mutation releases the lock. That violates the required ordering to stop accepting new connections first and leaves a race window for new work to enter shutdown.

`killAllChildProcesses()` only cleans up `automationState.process`, `workflowWorkers`, and `profileProcesses`. Other Python children spawned through `ProcessService` are never registered there, including the login subprocess started by `/api/automation/login` (`server/automation/routes.ts:98-100`, `server/automation/routes.ts:212-217`) and the fingerprint generator subprocess in `server/profiles/service.ts:61-65`. Because `spawnPython()` defaults to detached children on non-Windows platforms (`server/shared/ProcessService.ts:125-128`), those omitted processes can survive server exit, so the implementation does not satisfy “all Python child processes” / “no orphaned processes after server exit”.

`persistAutomationState()` snapshots `status`/`pid` before cleanup, rewrites `startedAt` to the shutdown time, drops `settings`, and the shutdown path never clears or rewrites the state file after `automationState.status` is set back to `'idle'` (`server/automation/shutdown.ts:157-159`). On the next boot, `handleInterruptedRun()` (`server/index.ts:159-177`) will treat a clean signal-driven shutdown of an active run as an interrupted session and immediately clear it. Recovery still works, but the persisted state is not an accurate final snapshot.

sharedStateObservations.observation: `refactor-worker` says new functionality should get tests in the red phase, but this feature changed shutdown orchestration/state persistence without adding any tests and still reported `followedProcedure: true`.
sharedStateObservations.evidence: `.factory/skills/refactor-worker/SKILL.md` Step 3 requires tests first for new functionality; the transcript skeleton for worker session `12cf5fef-3925-4eb3-9922-4d28948424dc` shows edits to `server/automation/state.ts`, `server/automation/shutdown.ts`, and `server/index.ts` before any test creation, and the handoff records `tests.added: []` plus `skillFeedback.followedProcedure: true`.

sharedStateObservations.observation: The shared service catalog only exposes force-stop helpers for the server, not a reusable graceful-shutdown exercise for SIGTERM/SIGINT or an orphan-process check, which makes reliability shutdown features easy to under-verify.
sharedStateObservations.evidence: `.factory/services.yaml` defines `stop_server_exec_safe` and `services.server.stop` with `Stop-Process -Force` on port 3001, but there is no companion command for sending a graceful signal and then checking that child Python processes are gone.

summary: Reviewed the feature metadata, handoff, transcript skeleton, skill instructions, shared-state artifacts, and commit `ccbf9eeb1dbb048ce7ad6fd645a42728286d30b4`. The review fails because shutdown still waits on the mutex before closing listeners and leaves some ProcessService-spawned Python children outside the cleanup set, so the implementation does not yet fully meet the graceful-shutdown/no-orphan requirements.
